examples.problem_statement: Which of the following are factors of 18? Indicate all such factors. (A) 2 (B) 3 (C) 6 (D) 12 (E) 18 (F) 36

solution.operation: \text{choice } n \text{ is a factor of } 18 \iff 18 \div n \in \mathbb{Z}
solution.result: test rule: divide 18 by the choice and check for an integer
solution.description: Set up the test the book uses: take 18 and divide it by each answer choice; an integer result means that choice is a factor.

solution.result: 9, an integer, so 2 is a factor
solution.description: Apply the test to choice (A) by dividing 18 by 2; the quotient is a whole number, so 2 qualifies.

solution.result: 6, an integer, so 3 is a factor
solution.description: Apply the test to choice (B) by dividing 18 by 3; the quotient is a whole number, so 3 qualifies.

solution.result: 3, an integer, so 6 is a factor
solution.description: Apply the test to choice (C) by dividing 18 by 6; the quotient is a whole number, so 6 qualifies.

solution.result: 1.5, not an integer, so 12 is not a factor
solution.description: Apply the test to choice (D) by dividing 18 by 12; the quotient is not a whole number, so 12 is rejected.

solution.result: 1, an integer, so 18 is a factor
solution.description: Apply the test to choice (E) by dividing 18 by itself; the quotient 1 is a whole number, so 18 qualifies.

solution.result: 0.5, not an integer, so 36 is not a factor
solution.description: Apply the test to choice (F) by dividing 18 by 36; the quotient is less than 1 and not a whole number, so 36 is rejected.

solution.result: the choices that passed the division test
solution.description: Collect every choice whose division produced an integer; on an all-that-apply question each surviving choice must be selected.

key_reminders: n is a factor of 18 only when 18 \div n leaves no remainder.
A number is always a factor of itself, so 18 must be tested and kept.
Indicate-all questions require every passing choice to be selected, not just one.
common_mistakes: Treating 12 as a factor because 12 shares the digits and factors of 18's neighbours, when 18 \div 12 = 1.5 is not an integer.
Testing divisibility in the wrong direction, checking 36 \div 18 instead of 18 \div 36, and wrongly accepting 36 (a multiple, not a factor).

examples.problem_statement: The ratio of cheese to sauce for a single pizza is 1 cup to 1/2 cup. If Bob used 15 cups of sauce to make a number of pizzas, how many cups of cheese did he use on those pizzas?

solution.description: Work with the part-to-part ratio and attach an unknown multiplier x, so the actual amounts are 1x of cheese and one-half x of sauce.
Set the sauce expression equal to the actual sauce Bob used, 15 cups, which pins down the multiplier.
Solve for x by undoing the one-half, multiplying 15 by 2.
Read the cheese amount off the ratio: since cheese is 1x, the multiplier x is itself the number of cups of cheese.

key_reminders: A part-to-part ratio becomes actual amounts only after an unknown multiplier x is attached to each part.
The multiplier is found from the one quantity whose actual value is given.
When a part carries coefficient 1, that part's actual value equals the multiplier itself.
common_mistakes: Reversing the ratio and taking half of 15 to get 7.5 cups, which the book flags explicitly as the trap here.
Solving \tfrac{1}{2}x = 15 by dividing by 2 instead of multiplying by 2.

examples.problem_statement: In a graduating class of 236 students, 142 took algebra and 121 took chemistry. What is the greatest possible number of students that could have taken both algebra and chemistry?

solution.result: a Venn diagram of the given counts
solution.description: Translate the words into a figure, drawing one circle for algebra and one for chemistry, since the 142 and 121 given do not yet separate the overlap.

solution.result: redrawn diagram with the overlap split out
solution.description: Redraw the Venn diagram with the students who took both labelled x, so each circle's exclusive region is its total minus x.
Require both exclusive regions to be non-negative, since a region of the diagram cannot hold a negative number of students.
Combine the two bounds; the tighter one, coming from the smaller circle, is what actually limits x.

solution.result: x = 121 is attainable, so it is the greatest value
solution.description: Confirm nothing in the problem excludes x from reaching its bound, so the largest possible overlap is that bound itself.

key_reminders: Totals given for each group already include the overlap, so split the overlap out before reasoning.
Every region of a Venn diagram must hold a count of zero or more.
The overlap of two groups can never exceed the size of the smaller group.
common_mistakes: Using the class size 236 as a constraint on x, when the binding limit comes from the smaller subject total 121.
Applying 142 + 121 - 236 = 27 (the least possible overlap) as the answer to a greatest-possible question.
